column2: Britain has lost its foothold in the south. With the Cape secured, the republic can turn from the battlefield to the boundaries of its northern interests. Lisbon still looks across the interior towards the distant ports of Mozambique, seeking a road from Angola to the Indian Ocean. Our government recognises a Portuguese field of expansion north of the Zambezi, while affirming the republic's claims in Mashonaland and Matabeleland. Survey parties and trading stations may follow this understanding, but the rulers of the interior still command their own territories. A map drawn at a conference is only the beginning of the work ahead.
Let the Zambezi mark our respective interests.

The British withdrawal from southern Africa has changed the prospects of our inland policy. The South African government claims Mashonaland and Matabeleland, but recognises our ambitions north of the Zambezi. A chain of surveys, river stations and roads could join the Angolan interior to the approaches of Mozambique. Each expedition will require money, supplies and secure bases at both ends. Territories already governed by African rulers or foreign powers cannot simply be occupied under this understanding. Lisbon must now decide whether to finance the long journey across the continent.
Surveyors and caravan leaders propose an eastern route from Angola through the Barotse country. Fund stations in unclaimed districts while respecting the lands of established rulers.
